❓ Question 1 (Long Question - 10 marks): Define Iman (Faith) in Islam. Explain the six articles of faith (Iman-e-Mufassal) in detail.

📌 Answer:

Definition of Iman (Faith): Iman is the firm belief and conviction in the heart, affirmed by the tongue, and acted upon by the limbs. It is the foundation of Islam. The Holy Quran says: "The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts become fearful, and when His verses are recited to them, it increases them in faith; and upon their Lord they rely" (Surah Al-Anfal, 8:2).

The Six Articles of Faith (Iman-e-Mufassal):

  • 1. Belief in Allah (Tauheed): The most fundamental article is belief in the Oneness of Allah. He is the Creator, Sustainer, and Master of the universe. He has no partner, no son, no parents. He is All-Powerful, All-Knowing, and Most Merciful. The Quran states: "Say, He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent" (Surah Al-Ikhlas, 112:1-4).
  • 2. Belief in Angels (Mala'ikah): Angels are created by Allah from light (noor). They are sinless, obedient, and invisible. They perform various duties: Jibraeel (AS) brought revelation, Mika'eel (AS) controls rain and sustenance, Israfeel (AS) will blow the Trumpet on Judgment Day, and Azra'eel (AS) takes souls at death. Two angels (Kiraman Katibeen) record every person's deeds.
  • 3. Belief in Divine Books (Kutubullah): Allah revealed holy books to various prophets as guidance for humanity. These include: the Torah (Tawrat) to Musa (AS), the Psalms (Zabur) to Dawud (AS), the Gospel (Injeel) to Isa (AS), and the final, complete, and unchanged revelation—the Holy Quran—to Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). Muslims believe in all previous books but follow only the Quran as the final authority.
  • 4. Belief in Prophets (Rusulullah): Allah sent prophets to every nation to guide them to the right path. The first prophet was Adam (AS), and the last is Muhammad (ﷺ). There are 124,000 prophets according to Hadith, but 25 are mentioned in the Quran. Muslims believe in all prophets without discrimination. The Quran says: "We make no distinction between any of His messengers" (Surah Al-Baqarah, 2:285).
  • 5. Belief in the Day of Judgment (Yawm al-Qiyamah): This is belief in the final day when all humans will be resurrected for accountability. On that day, every person will be judged according to their deeds. Those with good deeds will enter Paradise (Jannah), and those with evil deeds will be punished in Hellfire (Jahannam). Belief in the afterlife encourages righteous behavior and accountability.
  • 6. Belief in Divine Decree (Qadr): Belief that everything—good or bad—happens by the will and knowledge of Allah. Allah has preordained everything, including life, death, wealth, and poverty. However, humans have free will to choose between right and wrong, and they will be held accountable for their choices. The Quran states: "Indeed, all things We created with predestination" (Surah Al-Qamar, 54:49).
📖 Quranic Reference: "The Messenger has believed in what was revealed to him from his Lord, and [so have] the believers. All of them have believed in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers, [saying], 'We make no distinction between any of His messengers.'" (Surah Al-Baqarah, 2:285)
❓ Question 2 (Long Question - 10 marks): Explain the five pillars of Islam (Arkan-e-Islam) in detail. What is the importance of each pillar?

📌 Answer:

Introduction: The five pillars of Islam are the foundation of a Muslim's faith and practice. Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) said: "Islam is built upon five [pillars]: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah; establishing prayer; giving Zakat; fasting Ramadan; and Hajj to the House (Kaaba)" (Bukhari & Muslim).

  • 1. Shahadah (Declaration of Faith): The first pillar is the declaration: "Ash-hadu an la ilaha illa Allah, wa ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasul-Allah" (I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah). This statement affirms the Oneness of Allah and the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is the entry point to Islam. Importance: It distinguishes a Muslim from a non-Muslim and is the basis of all other acts of worship.
  • 2. Salah (Prayer): Muslims perform five daily prayers: Fajr (dawn), Dhuhr (noon), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (sunset), and Isha (night). Prayer includes recitation of Quran, bowing (ruku), prostration (sajdah), and supplication (dua). Importance: Salah connects a Muslim directly to Allah five times a day, purifies the soul, prevents indecency and evil, and provides spiritual discipline. The Quran says: "Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing" (Surah Al-Ankabut, 29:45).
  • 3. Zakat (Almsgiving): Zakat is the compulsory charity of 2.5% of a Muslim's annual savings (wealth, gold, silver, cash, business assets) given to the poor and needy. It purifies wealth and helps reduce economic inequality. Importance: Zakat teaches compassion, generosity, and social responsibility. It is a right of the poor upon the rich. The Quran mentions Zakat alongside Salah many times, indicating its importance.
  • 4. Sawm (Fasting in Ramadan): Muslims fast from dawn to sunset during the month of Ramadan. Fasting means abstaining from food, drink, smoking, and sexual relations, as well as evil thoughts and actions. Importance: Fasting develops self-discipline, empathy for the hungry, spiritual purification, and gratitude to Allah. The Quran states: "O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed upon you as it was prescribed upon those before you, that you may become righteous" (Surah Al-Baqarah, 2:183).
  • 5. Hajj (Pilgrimage to Makkah): Hajj is obligatory once in a lifetime for every Muslim who is physically and financially able. It occurs during the 8th to 12th of Dhul-Hijjah. Pilgrims wear simple white garments (Ihram), perform Tawaf (circling the Kaaba), Sa'ee (walking between Safa and Marwa), stand at Arafat, and stone the devil. Importance: Hajj symbolizes unity, equality, and submission to Allah. It erases past sins and renews one's faith.
💡 Tutor's Advice: For 10 marks, explain each pillar with its Arabic name, description, and at least one Quranic verse or Hadith. Draw a simple diagram showing the five pillars as a building foundation—examiners love visual aids!
❓ Question 3 (Long Question - 8 marks): Write a detailed note on the importance and teachings of the Holy Quran.

📌 Answer:

Definition: The Holy Quran is the literal word of Allah, revealed to Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) through the angel Jibraeel (AS) over a period of 23 years. It is the final and complete revelation, and it is preserved in its original Arabic text without any change.

Importance of the Holy Quran:

  • Primary Source of Guidance: The Quran is the ultimate guide for all humanity in matters of faith, worship, morality, law, economics, politics, and social relations. It provides solutions to every human problem.
  • Last and Complete Revelation: Unlike previous scriptures that were altered, the Quran remains unchanged. Allah Himself promised its preservation: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Quran and indeed, We will be its guardian" (Surah Al-Hijr, 15:9).
  • Source of Law (Shariah): The Quran is the primary source of Islamic law. Together with the Sunnah of the Prophet (ﷺ), it forms the basis of Shariah, governing all aspects of a Muslim's life.
  • Spiritual Healing and Mercy: The Quran is a source of healing for spiritual and psychological ailments. It brings peace to the heart. Allah says: "And We send down of the Quran that which is healing and mercy for the believers" (Surah Al-Isra, 17:82).
  • Miracle of Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): The Quran is the greatest miracle given to the Prophet. Its linguistic excellence, scientific facts, historical accuracy, and prophecies prove its divine origin.

Major Teachings of the Holy Quran:

  • Tauheed (Oneness of Allah): The central message is that Allah alone is worthy of worship. No partners, no intermediaries.
  • Risalah (Prophethood): Belief in all prophets, especially Muhammad (ﷺ) as the final messenger.
  • Akhirah (Hereafter): Belief in the Day of Judgment, heaven, and hell.
  • Justice and Equality: The Quran emphasizes justice for all, regardless of race, color, or social status. "O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice" (Surah An-Nisa, 4:135).
  • Moral Virtues: Honesty, truthfulness, patience, forgiveness, humility, charity, and kindness to parents, orphans, and neighbors.
  • Prohibition of Evils: The Quran forbids shirk (polytheism), lying, cheating, murder, theft, adultery, alcohol, gambling, usury (interest), and oppression.
  • Human Dignity: "And We have certainly honored the children of Adam" (Surah Al-Isra, 17:70).
  • Knowledge and Reflection: The Quran repeatedly encourages learning, observation, and contemplation of the universe.
❓ Question 4 (Long Question - 10 marks): Discuss the concept of "Seerat-un-Nabi" (Life of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ). Explain the key characteristics of the Prophet (ﷺ) as a leader, a teacher, and a role model.

📌 Answer:

Definition of Seerat-un-Nabi: Seerat refers to the life, character, conduct, and teachings of Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). It includes his biography, his sayings (Hadith), his actions, and his approvals. The Quran commands Muslims to follow the Prophet's example: "Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day and remembers Allah often" (Surah Al-Ahzab, 33:21).

Key Characteristics of Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ):

  • As a Leader:
    • Truthfulness and Honesty: Even before prophethood, he was known as "Al-Amin" (the trustworthy). He never lied or cheated.
    • Consultation (Shura): He consulted his companions in matters of state and war, even though he received divine revelation. This teaches democratic leadership.
    • Justice and Equality: He treated all people equally, regardless of wealth or status. Once he said that if his own daughter Fatima stole, she would be punished.
    • Mercy and Forgiveness: After conquering Makkah, he forgave his worst enemies who had persecuted him for 13 years. This is unmatched in history.
  • As a Teacher:
    • Patience and Gentleness: He taught with kindness, never harshness. He said, "Make things easy, not difficult" (Bukhari).
    • Practical Demonstration: He taught by example. He prayed, fasted, gave charity, and interacted with people in front of his companions.
    • Use of Parables and Questions: He used stories and rhetorical questions to make concepts easy to understand.
    • Respect for Students: He listened attentively and never interrupted anyone. He would sit in a circle with his companions, treating everyone equally.
  • As a Role Model:
    • Worship and Devotion: He prayed at night until his feet swelled. He fasted regularly. He was deeply connected to Allah.
    • Family Life: He was an ideal husband and father. He helped with household chores, mended his own clothes, and treated his wives with kindness and respect.
    • Social Relations: He visited the sick, attended funerals, greeted children, and helped widows and orphans. He never rejected an invitation from the poor.
    • Business Ethics: As a merchant, he was known for fair dealings. He forbade cheating, hoarding, and false oaths.
    • Bravery and Patience: He faced persecution, boycotts, and wars with unwavering patience and trust in Allah. He never sought revenge.
🕌 Quranic Command: "And indeed, you are of a great moral character" (Surah Al-Qalam, 68:4). This verse summarizes the Prophet's (ﷺ) exemplary character.
❓ Question 5 (Long Question - 10 marks): Define Hadith. Explain the classification of Hadith (Sahih, Hasan, Da'if, Mawdu') and the importance of Hadith in Islamic law.

📌 Answer:

Definition of Hadith: Hadith refers to the sayings, actions, approvals, and descriptions of Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). While the Quran is the word of Allah, Hadith is the practical interpretation and explanation of the Quran by the Prophet (ﷺ).

Classification of Hadith: Based on authenticity, Hadith is classified into four main categories:

  • Sahih (Authentic): A Hadith with a continuous chain of narration (isnad) consisting of upright and precise narrators, free from any irregularity or defect. Example: Most Hadith in Sahih Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. These are used as primary sources of Islamic law.
  • Hasan (Good): A Hadith where the chain of narration is slightly less precise than Sahih, but still acceptable. The narrators may have minor memory issues but are not accused of lying. Example: Many Hadith in Sunan Abu Dawood, Tirmidhi. These can be used for legal rulings but with caution.
  • Da'if (Weak): A Hadith with a break in the chain or a narrator who is known to have a poor memory or is of questionable reliability. Da'if Hadith cannot be used as the basis for legal rulings but may be used for virtuous deeds or moral encouragement, with caution.
  • Mawdu' (Fabricated): A Hadith that is falsely attributed to the Prophet (ﷺ). It contains a known liar in the chain or contradicts established Quranic teachings. Mawdu' Hadith are completely rejected and cannot be used for any purpose.

Importance of Hadith in Islamic Law:

  • Explanation of the Quran: The Hadith explains the general verses of the Quran. For example, the Quran commands prayer but the Hadith explains the method, timings, and number of rak'ahs.
  • Source of Legislation (Second after Quran): The Quran itself commands Muslims to obey the Prophet: "And whatever the Messenger has given you, take; and what he has forbidden you, refrain from" (Surah Al-Hashr, 59:7).
  • Practical Implementation: Without Hadith, many Islamic practices (like how to perform Hajj, Zakat calculation, marriage contracts) would be incomplete.
  • Moral and Ethical Guidance: The Hadith provides detailed guidance on manners, social conduct, and personal development.
🎯 Examiner's Note: For full marks, mention the famous Hadith collections: Sahih Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abu Dawood, Sunan Tirmidhi, Sunan Nasa'i, Sunan Ibn Majah. Also, explain the difference between Hadith and Sunnah briefly.

❓ Question 1 (Long Question - 10 marks): Define Ideology. Discuss the ideological basis of Pakistan in detail.

📌 Answer:

Definition of Ideology: An ideology is a comprehensive and coherent set of beliefs, ideas, values, and principles that guides the political and social actions of a nation. It provides a framework for understanding the world and a blueprint for collective action. The ideology of Pakistan is based on the Two-Nation Theory, which asserted that Muslims of the Indian subcontinent are a distinct nation and deserve a separate homeland where they can live according to Islamic principles.

Ideological Basis of Pakistan:

  • The Two-Nation Theory: The fundamental basis of Pakistan's ideology is the belief that Hindus and Muslims are two distinct nations. They differ in religion, culture, customs, traditions, language, and social values. Sir Syed Ahmed Khan first articulated this idea after the 1857 War of Independence. He realized that Hindus and Muslims could not live together peacefully. Allama Iqbal gave this concept a political shape in his 1930 Allahabad Address, where he proposed a separate Muslim state in Northwestern India. Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah further elaborated the Two-Nation Theory and led the struggle for Pakistan.
  • Islamic Principles: The ideology of Pakistan is deeply rooted in Islam. The Muslims of the subcontinent wanted a state where they could practice their religion freely and live according to Islamic teachings. The Objectives Resolution (1949) laid down the principles of an Islamic democratic state where sovereignty belongs to Allah Almighty, and the state exercises its powers through the people as a sacred trust.
  • Democratic System: Pakistan's ideology promotes democracy, justice, and equality. The state is committed to providing equal rights to all citizens regardless of religion, caste, or creed. Non-Muslims have full freedom to practice their religion and participate in national affairs.
  • Cultural Identity: The ideology of Pakistan emphasizes the preservation and promotion of Islamic culture and heritage. It rejects the Hindu-dominated culture of India and aims to create a distinct Muslim identity.
  • Social Justice: Pakistan's ideology promotes social justice, equality, and fraternity. It rejects exploitation and discrimination. The state is responsible for ensuring the welfare of all citizens, especially the poor and marginalized.
📊 Key Point: The ideology of Pakistan is a combination of Islamic principles and democratic values. It is based on the belief that Muslims are a separate nation and deserve a homeland where they can live according to their faith and culture.
❓ Question 2 (Long Question - 10 marks): Write a detailed note on the Pakistan Resolution (Lahore Resolution) of 1940. What was its significance in the creation of Pakistan?

📌 Answer:

Background: The Pakistan Resolution, also known as the Lahore Resolution, was a landmark political statement passed by the All-India Muslim League during its three-day general session held at Minto Park (now Iqbal Park) in Lahore on March 22-24, 1940. The resolution was drafted by the Muslim League's Working Committee and presented by A.K. Fazlul Haq, the then Chief Minister of Bengal.

Text of the Resolution: The resolution declared that "no constitutional plan would be workable or acceptable to the Muslims unless geographical contiguous units are demarcated into regions which should be constituted as Independent States in which the constituent units shall be autonomous and sovereign." It specifically mentioned the Northwestern and Eastern zones of the subcontinent where Muslims were in majority.

Significance of the Pakistan Resolution:

  • Clear Demand for a Separate Homeland: For the first time, the Muslim League explicitly demanded a separate Muslim state. It marked the shift from seeking safeguards within a united India to demanding a sovereign Muslim nation.
  • Mobilization of Muslims: The resolution energized the Muslim masses across the subcontinent. It gave them a clear goal and a reason to support the Muslim League.
  • Rejection of Federal Plans: The resolution rejected the idea of a single federal India where Muslims would be a permanent minority. It asserted that Muslims are a separate nation and deserve self-determination.
  • Foundation of Pakistan Movement: The Lahore Resolution became the cornerstone of the Pakistan Movement. It guided the Muslim League's political strategy for the next seven years, leading to the creation of Pakistan on August 14, 1947.
  • International Recognition: The resolution put the Muslim demand on the international stage. It forced the British government to consider the partition of India as a possible solution to the Hindu-Muslim problem.
💡 Tutor's Advice: For 10 marks, mention the exact date (March 23, 1940) and place (Minto Park, Lahore). Explain how this resolution later became known as the "Pakistan Resolution" even though the word "Pakistan" was not used in the original text. This is a guaranteed question in almost every AIOU Pakistan Studies exam!
❓ Question 3 (Long Question - 8 marks): Write a comprehensive note on the services and contributions of Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah for the creation of Pakistan.

📌 Answer:

Introduction: Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah (1876-1948) was the founder of Pakistan and the leader of the Muslim League. His tireless efforts, political wisdom, and unwavering determination led to the creation of a separate homeland for the Muslims of the subcontinent. He is revered as the "Father of the Nation."

Contributions of Quaid-e-Azam:

  • Joining the Muslim League (1913): Jinnah joined the Muslim League in 1913. Initially, he was a member of the Indian National Congress and advocated for Hindu-Muslim unity. However, he realized that Congress was pursuing a Hindu agenda that would marginalize Muslims. He dedicated himself fully to the Muslim League after 1930.
  • Fourteen Points (1929): In response to the Nehru Report (1928), Jinnah presented his Fourteen Points. These points outlined the minimum safeguards required for Muslims in any future constitution. They included separate electorates, one-third Muslim representation in the Central Legislature, and provincial autonomy. The Fourteen Points became the basis of Muslim political demands.
  • Reorganization of the Muslim League (1935-1937): After the 1937 elections, Jinnah reorganized the Muslim League, transforming it from a party of elite Muslims into a mass movement. He traveled extensively, addressing public meetings and mobilizing support for the League.
  • Pakistan Resolution (1940): Jinnah led the Muslim League to pass the Pakistan Resolution in Lahore in 1940. He argued that Muslims are a separate nation and deserve a homeland where they can live according to Islamic principles.
  • Leadership during the Cripps Mission (1942) and Cabinet Mission (1946): Jinnah skillfully negotiated with the British government and the Congress. He rejected the Cripps Mission proposals because they did not guarantee a separate Muslim state. He also rejected the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) because it did not provide adequate safeguards for Muslims.
  • Direct Action Day (1946): When the Congress rejected the Muslim League's demands, Jinnah called for Direct Action Day on August 16, 1946, to press for the demand for Pakistan. This led to widespread communal violence but also forced the British to accept the inevitability of partition.
  • Negotiations for Partition (1947): Jinnah represented the Muslim League in the final negotiations with Lord Mountbatten and the Congress. He successfully secured a separate state for Muslims, despite the Congress's initial opposition.
  • Founding Father of Pakistan: After the creation of Pakistan on August 14, 1947, Jinnah became the first Governor-General. He worked tirelessly to establish the new state, addressing its early challenges, including the refugee crisis, economic instability, and constitutional issues. He famously outlined his vision for Pakistan in his August 11, 1947 speech: "You may belong to any religion, caste or creed—that has nothing to do with the business of the state."
🎯 Examiner's Note: For full marks, include key dates (1913, 1929, 1940, 1947) and emphasize Jinnah's leadership qualities. This question often appears in both short and long forms. Memorize at least 6-7 points for a 10-mark answer.
❓ Question 4 (Long Question - 10 marks): Explain the Geographical Importance of Pakistan. Discuss its location, boundaries, and strategic significance.

📌 Answer:

Location of Pakistan: Pakistan is located in South Asia, between latitudes 23° 30' to 36° 45' North and longitudes 61° to 75° 30' East. It covers an area of approximately 796,096 square kilometers, making it the 33rd largest country in the world.

Boundaries of Pakistan:

  • North and Northeast: China (through the Karakoram Highway and Khunjerab Pass) and India (Line of Control in Kashmir).
  • East: India (Rajasthan, Punjab, and Gujarat).
  • West and Southwest: Afghanistan (Durand Line) and Iran (Makran Coast).
  • South: Arabian Sea, with a coastline of about 1,046 kilometers.

Geographical Importance of Pakistan:

  • Gateway to Central Asia: Pakistan is strategically located at the crossroads of South Asia, Central Asia, and the Middle East. It serves as a land bridge between the energy-rich Central Asian republics (Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan) and the warm waters of the Arabian Sea. This makes Pakistan a vital transit route for trade and energy supplies.
  • Significance of Gwadar Port: Gwadar Port, located on the Makran Coast, is a deep-sea port that provides Pakistan with access to the Indian Ocean. It is a key component of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). Gwadar is strategically located near the Strait of Hormuz, through which about 20% of the world's oil passes. It gives China and other Central Asian countries an alternative route for trade, reducing their dependence on the Malacca Strait.
  • China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC): CPEC is a mega-project that connects Gwadar Port to China's Xinjiang province via roads, railways, and pipelines. It enhances Pakistan's strategic importance by linking it to China's Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). CPEC includes energy projects, infrastructure development, and industrial zones, which are transforming Pakistan's economy.
  • Natural Resources: Pakistan's geography provides it with abundant natural resources, including fertile agricultural lands (Indus River Basin), minerals (coal, copper, gold, gypsum), and energy resources (natural gas, hydropower, solar, wind).
  • Strategic Depth: Pakistan's northern areas (Gilgit-Baltistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) provide strategic depth in case of conflict with India. The mountainous terrain makes it difficult for invading forces to penetrate.
  • Trade Routes: Pakistan has historically been a trade route for civilizations. The Indus Valley Civilization flourished along the Indus River. Today, Pakistan is part of several trade corridors, including the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) and the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC).
📊 Key Point: Pakistan's location at the confluence of three major regions—South Asia, Central Asia, and the Middle East—gives it immense strategic and economic importance. The development of Gwadar Port and CPEC has further enhanced Pakistan's role as a regional trade hub.
❓ Question 5 (Long Question - 10 marks): Discuss the constitutional developments in Pakistan from 1947 to 1973. Describe the main features of the 1973 Constitution.

📌 Answer:

Constitutional Developments (1947-1973):

  • Interim Constitution (1947-1956): After independence, Pakistan adopted the Government of India Act 1935 as an interim constitution, with necessary amendments. The Constituent Assembly was tasked with framing a new constitution.
  • Objectives Resolution (1949): The Constituent Assembly, led by Prime Minister Liaquat Ali Khan, passed the Objectives Resolution on March 12, 1949. It laid down the principles of an Islamic democratic state: sovereignty belongs to Allah Almighty, the state will exercise its powers through the people as a sacred trust, and Muslims will be able to live according to Islamic principles. The resolution became the preamble of all subsequent constitutions.
  • Constitution of 1956: Pakistan's first constitution was enacted on March 23, 1956. It established Pakistan as the Islamic Republic of Pakistan. It provided for a parliamentary system with a President as the head of state and a Prime Minister as the head of government. However, this constitution was short-lived as General Ayub Khan imposed martial law in 1958.
  • Constitution of 1962: General Ayub Khan introduced the 1962 Constitution on June 8, 1962. It established a presidential system with a strong executive president. It introduced the concept of "Basic Democracies" (indirect elections). This constitution was also short-lived and was abrogated after Ayub Khan's resignation in 1969.
  • Interim Period (1969-1972): General Yahya Khan imposed martial law and held the first general elections in 1970. After the fall of East Pakistan (Bangladesh) in 1971, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto took over and initiated the process of framing a new constitution.

Constitution of 1973 (Main Features):

  • Parliamentary System: The 1973 Constitution established a parliamentary system with a Prime Minister as the head of government and a President as the head of state (ceremonial role).
  • Federal System: Pakistan is a federation with four provinces: Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Balochistan. It also includes Gilgit-Baltistan, Azad Kashmir, and the Islamabad Capital Territory.
  • Bicameral Legislature: The Parliament consists of two houses: the National Assembly (lower house) and the Senate (upper house). The National Assembly represents the people, while the Senate represents the provinces.
  • Islamic Provisions: The constitution declares Islam as the state religion. It requires that all laws be consistent with the Quran and Sunnah. It establishes the Council of Islamic Ideology to advise the government on Islamic matters.
  • Fundamental Rights: The constitution guarantees fundamental rights to all citizens, including equality before the law, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, and right to life and liberty.
  • Independent Judiciary: The constitution provides for an independent judiciary with the Supreme Court as the apex court. The Chief Justice is appointed by the President.
  • Directive Principles of State Policy: The constitution outlines principles for governance, including promoting social welfare, reducing inequality, and protecting the environment.
🔑 Important Tip: The 1973 Constitution is the current constitution of Pakistan. It has been amended several times (e.g., 8th Amendment by Zia-ul-Haq, 18th Amendment by PPP in 2010). For exams, focus on the key features of the 1973 Constitution and the main differences between the 1956, 1962, and 1973 constitutions.

❓ Question 1 (Long Question - 10 marks): Define Information and Communication Technology (ICT). Explain the applications of ICT in various fields of life with suitable examples.

📌 Answer:

Definition of ICT: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) refers to all technologies used to handle telecommunications, broadcast media, intelligent building management systems, audiovisual processing and transmission systems, and network-based control and monitoring functions. It is an extended term for Information Technology (IT) that emphasizes the role of unified communications and the integration of telecommunications (telephone lines and wireless signals), computers, necessary enterprise software, middleware, storage, and audiovisual systems.

Applications of ICT in Various Fields:

  • Education: E-learning platforms, online courses, virtual classrooms, digital libraries. Example: AIOU's own Learning Management System (LMS) for online lectures and assignments.
  • Business: E-commerce, online banking, video conferencing, customer relationship management (CRM). Example: Daraz.pk and other online shopping platforms.
  • Healthcare: Telemedicine, electronic health records (EHR), medical imaging, robotic surgeries. Example: Sehat Kahani and other telemedicine apps in Pakistan.
  • Government (E-Governance): Online tax filing (FBR), digital identity systems (NADRA), online passport applications. Example: Pakistan Citizen's Portal for complaint registration.
  • Banking & Finance: ATM machines, online banking apps, mobile wallets (JazzCash, Easypaisa), cryptocurrency.
  • Agriculture: Precision farming, weather forecasting apps, market price information systems, drone-based crop monitoring.
  • Entertainment: Streaming services (Netflix, YouTube), online gaming, social media platforms (Facebook, Instagram, TikTok).
  • Transportation: GPS navigation (Google Maps), ride-hailing apps (Uber, Careem), traffic management systems, airline reservation systems.
💡 Tutor's Advice: For 10 marks, explain each point with a relevant Pakistani example. Examiners love when you relate concepts to the local context. Draw a small diagram showing how ICT connects different fields!
❓ Question 2 (Long Question - 10 marks): Define the term "Computer". Describe the five generations of computers in detail, highlighting the key technologies used in each generation.

📌 Answer:

Definition of Computer: A computer is an electronic device that accepts data (input), processes it according to a set of instructions (program), produces information (output), and stores results for future use. It operates under the control of instructions stored in its own memory.

Five Generations of Computers:

  • First Generation (1940-1956): Vacuum Tubes
    - Technology: Used vacuum tubes as the basic components for memory and circuitry.
    - Features: Very large in size (occupied entire rooms), produced excessive heat, consumed huge amounts of electricity, unreliable, expensive.
    - Examples: ENIAC, EDVAC, UNIVAC-1.
    - Languages: Machine language (0s and 1s) and assembly language.
  • Second Generation (1956-1963): Transistors
    - Technology: Replaced vacuum tubes with transistors (invented at Bell Labs).
    - Features: Smaller, faster, more reliable, produced less heat, consumed less power, more portable.
    - Examples: IBM 1401, IBM 1620, UNIVAC 1107.
    - Languages: High-level languages like FORTRAN and COBOL emerged.
  • Third Generation (1964-1971): Integrated Circuits (ICs)
    - Technology: Multiple transistors were placed on a single silicon chip (IC).
    - Features: Even smaller, cheaper, faster, more reliable, lower power consumption.
    - Examples: IBM System/360, PDP-8, PDP-11.
    - Languages: Operating systems became common; keyboards and monitors replaced punch cards.
  • Fourth Generation (1971-1980): Microprocessors
    - Technology: Thousands of ICs were combined on a single chip (microprocessor). Intel 4004 was the first microprocessor.
    - Features: Very small (personal computers), inexpensive, graphical user interfaces (GUIs), networking capabilities.
    - Examples: Apple II, IBM PC, Commodore PET.
    - Languages: C, C++, Pascal, and other high-level languages became popular.
  • Fifth Generation (1980-Present): Artificial Intelligence (AI)
    - Technology: Uses ULSI (Ultra Large Scale Integration) technology, parallel processing, and AI.
    - Features: Natural language processing, expert systems, robotics, voice recognition, portable devices (laptops, smartphones, tablets).
    - Examples: Desktops, laptops, smartphones, tablets, AI assistants (Siri, Google Assistant).
    - Languages: Python, Java, JavaScript, C#, and other modern languages.
📊 Quick Summary: Computer Generations in a Nutshell:
1st: Vacuum Tubes 🟰 ENIAC
2nd: Transistors 🟰 Smaller
3rd: ICs 🟰 Cheaper
4th: Microprocessors 🟰 Personal Computers
5th: AI & ULSI 🟰 Smart Devices
❓ Question 3 (Long Question - 8 marks): Differentiate between Hardware and Software. Explain the different types of computer software with examples.

📌 Answer:

Hardware vs. Software:

  • Hardware: The physical, touchable components of a computer system (e.g., CPU, monitor, keyboard, mouse, printer, hard disk).
  • Software: The set of instructions or programs that tell the hardware what to do (e.g., Windows, MS Office, games, browsers).

Types of Computer Software:

1. System Software: Software that controls and manages the basic operations of a computer system. It acts as an interface between hardware and application software.

  • Operating System (OS): Manages all hardware and other software. Examples: Microsoft Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS.
  • Device Drivers: Allow the OS to communicate with hardware devices. Example: Printer driver, graphics card driver.
  • Utility Programs: Perform specific tasks related to computer maintenance. Examples: Antivirus software, disk cleanup tools, file compression tools (WinRAR).
  • Language Translators: Convert high-level programming language code into machine language. Examples: Compiler, interpreter, assembler.

2. Application Software: Software designed to help users perform specific tasks or applications.

  • Word Processors: Examples: MS Word, Google Docs, Notepad.
  • Spreadsheets: Examples: MS Excel, Google Sheets.
  • Presentation Software: Examples: MS PowerPoint, Google Slides.
  • Database Software: Examples: MS Access, Oracle, MySQL.
  • Web Browsers: Examples: Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Safari.
  • Email Clients: Examples: Microsoft Outlook, Mozilla Thunderbird.
  • Graphics & Design Software: Examples: Adobe Photoshop, CorelDRAW, Canva.
  • Games & Entertainment: Examples: PUBG, Free Fire, Candy Crush.
❓ Question 4 (Long Question - 10 marks): What is an Operating System? Explain the major functions of an operating system in detail.

📌 Answer:

Definition of Operating System: An operating system (OS) is a collection of system software that manages computer hardware resources and provides common services for computer programs. It is the most important software that runs on a computer. Without an operating system, a computer is useless. Examples: Microsoft Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS.

Major Functions of an Operating System:

  • Process Management: The OS manages the execution of multiple processes (programs in execution). It allocates CPU time to processes, creates and terminates processes, and handles process scheduling and synchronization. Example: When you open MS Word, a browser, and a media player simultaneously, the OS manages which program gets CPU time and for how long.
  • Memory Management: The OS manages the computer's primary memory (RAM). It keeps track of which parts of memory are being used and by which process, allocates memory to processes when they request it, and deallocates memory when processes are finished. Example: When you open a new application, the OS finds free space in RAM and loads the application there.
  • File Management: The OS manages files on storage devices (hard disk, SSD, USB drives). It organizes files into directories/folders, provides file access permissions, and handles file creation, deletion, renaming, and copying operations. Example: Windows Explorer allows you to browse, create, and manage files and folders.
  • Device Management (I/O Management): The OS manages input and output devices (keyboard, mouse, printer, monitor, etc.). It uses device drivers to communicate with hardware devices and handles I/O requests from processes. Example: When you press a key on the keyboard, the OS receives the signal and passes it to the active application.
  • Security & Protection: The OS protects user data and prevents unauthorized access. It implements user authentication (usernames/passwords), file permissions, and protects processes from interfering with each other. Example: Windows login screen and user account control (UAC) features.
  • User Interface (UI): The OS provides an interface between the user and the computer hardware. This can be a Command-Line Interface (CLI) like MS-DOS or a Graphical User Interface (GUI) like Windows.
  • Error Detection & Handling: The OS constantly monitors the system for errors (hardware failures, software bugs) and takes appropriate action to maintain system stability. Example: "Blue Screen of Death" (BSOD) in Windows or error messages when a program crashes.
  • Resource Allocation: The OS allocates system resources (CPU, memory, I/O devices) among multiple users or processes to ensure efficient and fair usage.
❓ Question 5 (Long Question - 10 marks): What is a Computer Network? Explain different types of network topologies with suitable diagrams and examples.

📌 Answer:

Definition of Computer Network: A computer network is a group of interconnected computing devices (computers, servers, printers, smartphones, etc.) that can communicate and share resources with each other. The primary purposes of a network are resource sharing (files, printers, internet connection), communication (email, chat, video calls), and centralized data management.

Types of Network Topologies:

  • Bus Topology: All devices are connected to a single central cable (called the bus or backbone).
    - Advantages: Inexpensive, easy to install, requires less cable.
    - Disadvantages: If the main cable fails, the entire network fails; performance degrades with more devices.
    - Example: Small office or school lab networks in the past.
  • Star Topology: All devices are connected to a central hub or switch. The hub acts as a central connection point.
    - Advantages: Easy to install and manage; if one cable fails, only that device is affected; high performance.
    - Disadvantages: If the central hub fails, the entire network fails; requires more cable than bus topology.
    - Example: Most home and office networks (Wi-Fi routers act as central hubs).
  • Ring Topology: Each device is connected to two other devices, forming a closed loop or ring. Data travels in one direction (or both directions in a dual ring).
    - Advantages: Data transmission is predictable; handles high traffic well.
    - Disadvantages: If one device or cable fails, the entire network fails (unless a dual ring is used); difficult to troubleshoot.
    - Example: Older IBM token ring networks.
  • Mesh Topology: Every device is connected to every other device in the network.
    - Advantages: Highly fault-tolerant (multiple paths for data); no single point of failure.
    - Disadvantages: Very expensive and complex to install and maintain; requires a lot of cabling.
    - Example: Military networks, large banking networks, or the Internet backbone.
  • Tree (Hierarchical) Topology: A combination of bus and star topologies. It has a root node and multiple levels of star-configured networks.
    - Advantages: Scalable (easily expandable); easy to manage and maintain.
    - Disadvantages: If the root node fails, the entire network fails; requires more cabling.
    - Example: Large corporate networks or university campus networks.
📐 Quick Tip for Exams: For full marks in long questions, always draw neat labeled diagrams of each topology. Examiners are impressed by visual representations!

❓ Question 1 (Long Question - 10 marks): Define Statistics. Explain the scope and limitations of Statistics in business decision-making.

📌 Answer:

Definition of Statistics: Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, analyzing, interpreting, and presenting data to make informed decisions. In business, it helps managers understand trends, predict future outcomes, and minimize risks.

Scope of Statistics in Business:

  • Marketing: Analyzing consumer behavior, market research, and sales forecasting.
  • Finance: Risk analysis, portfolio management, and investment decisions.
  • Production: Quality control, inventory management, and process optimization.
  • Human Resources: Employee performance evaluation and workforce planning.
  • Strategic Planning: Using historical data to set realistic goals and budgets.

Limitations of Statistics:

  • Does not study individuals: Statistics deals with aggregates, not single items.
  • Can be misused: Incorrect data or biased sampling leads to wrong conclusions.
  • Requires expert handling: Proper interpretation needs statistical knowledge.
  • Only quantitative data: Qualitative factors (like employee morale) are hard to measure.
  • Results are probabilistic: Statistical findings are never 100% certain; they provide probabilities.
💡 Tutor's Advice: For 10 marks, explain each point with a real-world business example. Draw a neat table comparing scope vs limitations. Examiners love structured answers!
❓ Question 2 (Long Question - 10 marks): Calculate the Mean, Median, and Mode from the following data:
12, 15, 18, 22, 22, 25, 28, 30, 32, 35. Also, identify which measure of central tendency is most appropriate for this data.

📌 Step-by-Step Solution:

Given Data: 12, 15, 18, 22, 22, 25, 28, 30, 32, 35 (n = 10)

1. Mean (Arithmetic Average):
Mean = (Sum of all values) / n
Sum = 12+15+18+22+22+25+28+30+32+35 = 239
Mean = 239 / 10 = 23.9

2. Median (Middle Value):
Since n=10 (even), Median = average of (n/2)th and (n/2 +1)th values.
5th value = 22, 6th value = 25
Median = (22 + 25)/2 = 23.5

3. Mode (Most Frequent Value):
The value 22 appears twice. All others appear once.
Mode = 22

Most Appropriate Measure: The Median is most appropriate here because the data has a slight skew (mean > median), and median is resistant to outliers. However, for business decisions, mean is commonly used for normally distributed data.

📐 Formulas: Mean = Σx / n   |   Median = (n+1)/2th term   |   Mode = most frequent value
❓ Question 3 (Long Question - 8 marks): Explain different types of graphs used in frequency distribution. Highlight their importance in business data analysis.

📌 Answer: Frequency distribution graphs visually represent how often each value occurs in a dataset. They are crucial for business presentations and trend analysis[reference:1].

Types of Graphs:

  • Histogram: A bar chart showing continuous data. Bars touch each other. Use: Employee salary distribution.
  • Bar Chart: Displays categorical data with separated bars. Use: Comparing sales across products.
  • Pie Chart: Circular chart showing proportions. Use: Market share analysis.
  • Frequency Polygon: Line graph connecting midpoints of histogram bars. Use: Tracking monthly sales trends.
  • Ogive (Cumulative Frequency Curve): Shows cumulative frequencies. Use: Finding percentiles, quartiles.

Importance in Business:

  • Quick Insights: Graphs reveal patterns that numbers hide.
  • Decision Making: Managers grasp trends faster through visuals.
  • Reporting: Professional charts enhance presentations.
  • Forecasting: Historical patterns help predict future performance.
🎯 Examiner's Note: For full marks, draw small rough sketches of each graph in your exam sheet. Neat diagrams with proper labels impress evaluators.
❓ Question 4 (Long Question - 10 marks): Differentiate between Sample and Population. Discuss the merits and demerits of sampling in business research.

📌 Answer: Understanding the difference between population and sample is fundamental to business statistics.

Definitions:
Population: The entire group under study (e.g., all customers of a company).
Sample: A subset of the population selected for analysis (e.g., 500 customers).

Merits of Sampling (Why we use samples):

  • Economical: Sampling requires fewer resources, reducing costs[reference:2].
  • Time-Saving: Studying a sample is faster, especially for large populations[reference:3].
  • Feasibility: Practical when the population is too large for complete enumeration[reference:4].
  • Efficiency: Data analysis is easier with smaller datasets[reference:5].
  • Reduced Workload: Focus on fewer data points ensures better quality[reference:6].

Demerits of Sampling (Limitations):

  • Sampling Errors: The process may lead to bias or incorrect inferences[reference:7].
  • Non-Representativeness: If sample isn't representative, results are misleading[reference:8].
  • Limited Accuracy: Results can differ from actual population due to random variation[reference:9].
  • Not Suitable for Small Populations: Complete enumeration is better when population is small[reference:10].
  • Dependence on Sampling Method: Reliability heavily depends on the technique used[reference:11].
📊 Key Insight: A well-chosen sample can accurately represent a population with 95%+ confidence.
❓ Question 5 (Long Question - 10 marks): Define Primary and Secondary Data. Distinguish between them with suitable examples. Also explain their sources in business context.

📌 Answer: Data is the raw material of statistics. It is classified into two main types[reference:12].

Primary Data: Data collected directly by the researcher for a specific purpose[reference:13].

  • Sources: Surveys, questionnaires, interviews, experiments, direct observation[reference:14].
  • Example: A company conducting a customer satisfaction survey to understand its service quality[reference:15].

Secondary Data: Data collected and published by others for purposes other than the current research[reference:16].

  • Sources: Government reports (census), published research papers, business reports, online databases[reference:17].
  • Example: Using a market research report to analyze industry trends.

Differences between Primary and Secondary Data:

  • Originality: Primary is original; Secondary is already collected.
  • Time/Cost: Primary is time-consuming and expensive; Secondary is quick and cheap.
  • Accuracy: Primary is more accurate and relevant; Secondary may be outdated.
  • Control: Researcher has full control over primary data; No control over secondary data.
  • Purpose: Primary is collected for a specific problem; Secondary was collected for another purpose.

❓ Question 1 (Long Question - 8 marks): Define Matrix. Explain the types of matrices with at least one example for each.

📌 Answer: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers, symbols, or expressions arranged in rows and columns. It is denoted by a capital letter (e.g., A). It is a fundamental tool in business mathematics for solving systems of linear equations, input-output analysis, and data representation.

Types of Matrices with Examples:

  • Row Matrix: A matrix with only one row. Example: A = [2 5 8]
  • Column Matrix: A matrix with only one column. Example: B = [4; 7; 1]
  • Square Matrix: A matrix where the number of rows equals the number of columns. Example: C = |1 2; 3 4| (2x2 matrix)
  • Diagonal Matrix: A square matrix where all non-diagonal elements are zero. Example: D = |5 0; 0 9|
  • Identity Matrix: A diagonal matrix where all diagonal elements are 1. Example: I = |1 0; 0 1|
  • Zero/Null Matrix: A matrix where all elements are zero. Example: O = |0 0; 0 0|
  • Transpose of a Matrix: Obtained by interchanging rows and columns. If A = |a b; c d|, then Aᵀ = |a c; b d|.

🎓 Tutor's Advice: In exams, always draw a proper bracket [ ] or ( ) for matrices. For 8 marks, explain at least 6 types with neat examples. This is a guaranteed question!

❓ Question 2 (Long Question - 8 marks): A retailer bought 50 units of a product at Rs. 400 per unit. He marked the price 30% above the cost price and offered a 15% discount on the marked price. Calculate:
  • (a) The marked price per unit.
  • (b) The selling price per unit after discount.
  • (c) The total profit or loss on the whole sale.
  • (d) The percentage of profit or loss.

📌 Solution (Step-by-Step):

  1. Given Data:
    • Cost Price per unit (C.P) = Rs. 400
    • Mark-up on Cost Price = 30%
    • Discount on Marked Price = 15%
    • Total Units = 50
  2. (a) Marked Price (M.P):
    M.P = C.P + (30% of C.P) = 400 + (30/100 * 400) = 400 + 120 = Rs. 520 per unit.
  3. (b) Selling Price (S.P) after discount:
    Discount amount = 15% of M.P = (15/100) * 520 = Rs. 78.
    S.P = M.P - Discount = 520 - 78 = Rs. 442 per unit.
  4. (c) Total Profit or Loss:
    Total C.P = 50 * 400 = Rs. 20,000.
    Total S.P = 50 * 442 = Rs. 22,100.
    Since S.P > C.P, it's a Profit. Total Profit = 22,100 - 20,000 = Rs. 2,100.
  5. (d) Profit Percentage:
    Profit % = (Profit / Total C.P) * 100 = (2,100 / 20,000) * 100 = 10.5%.
💡 Examiner's Note: Always mention the formulas like M.P = C.P + Gain. Show your calculations clearly. This is a high-scoring question because it tests multiple concepts in one go.
❓ Question 3 (Short Question - 5 marks): Solve the system of linear equations using the substitution method: 2x + y = 10 and x - y = 2.

📌 Solution:

Given equations:
(1) 2x + y = 10
(2) x - y = 2

Step 1: From equation (2), we can write: x = 2 + y.

Step 2: Substitute this value of x into equation (1):
2(2 + y) + y = 10 → 4 + 2y + y = 10 → 4 + 3y = 10 → 3y = 6 → y = 2.

Step 3: Substitute y = 2 into x = 2 + y → x = 2 + 2 = 4.

Answer: x = 4, y = 2.

Verification: Put values in equation (1): 2(4) + 2 = 8 + 2 = 10. Correct!

❓ Question 4 (Long Question - 10 marks): Find the inverse of the following matrix using the adjoint method: A = | 2 3 ; 1 4 |

📌 Solution (Step-by-Step):

For a 2x2 matrix A = |a b; c d|, the inverse A⁻¹ = (1 / det(A)) * |d -b; -c a|.

Step 1: Calculate Determinant (det)
det(A) = (a*d) - (b*c) = (2*4) - (3*1) = 8 - 3 = 5.

Step 2: Find the Adjoint Matrix
The adjoint of A = |d -b; -c a| = |4 -3; -1 2|.

Step 3: Apply Formula for Inverse
A⁻¹ = (1/5) * |4 -3; -1 2| = |4/5 -3/5; -1/5 2/5|.

Final Answer: A⁻¹ = |0.8 -0.6; -0.2 0.4|.

🔑 Important Tip: Always verify by multiplying A * A⁻¹. The result should be the Identity Matrix (I). This is a common practice to check your answer in exams.
❓ Question 5 (Short Question - 5 marks): If the sum of the first 5 terms of an arithmetic sequence is 50 and the first term is 6, find the common difference.

📌 Solution:

Formula for sum of first n terms of an Arithmetic Progression (A.P): Sₙ = n/2 * [2a + (n-1)d].

Given: n = 5, S₅ = 50, a = 6.

Substitute values: 50 = 5/2 * [2(6) + (5-1)d] → 50 = 2.5 * [12 + 4d] → 50 / 2.5 = 12 + 4d → 20 = 12 + 4d → 20 - 12 = 4d → 8 = 4d → d = 2.

Answer: The common difference is 2. The sequence is: 6, 8, 10, 12, 14.

⚡ Short Questions for Quick Revision (Must Prepare)

  • Define Binary Operation with example.
  • What is the difference between Simple Interest and Compound Interest? Derive formulas.
  • Find the inverse of a 3x3 matrix (any standard matrix from your book).
  • Explain Cramer's Rule for solving equations.
  • Convert 0.75 into a percentage and ratio.
  • A man invests Rs. 5000 at 8% per annum. Find compound interest for 2 years.
  • Define Determinant. Calculate det of a 3x3 matrix.
🎓 Tutor's Final Word: These short questions cover the "heart" of Business Mathematics. If you master these 7 concepts, you can easily score 40+ out of 50 in the subjective part.

AIOU 1428 Solved Guess Paper 2026 | Commercial Geography Detailed Answers

AIOU ke tamaam ADC, B.Com aur BS Accounting & Finance ke students ke liye Commercial Geography (1428) ka paper bohat ahem hota hai. Bohat se students is subject ki complexity se pareshan hote hain. Isliye, Assignmentwaly ne aapki sahulat ke liye behtareen Solved Guess Paper 2026 tayyar kiya hai jo aapko 80%+ marks dilwane mein madad karega.

Q1: Define Commercial Geography and explain its relationship with other sciences.

Answer: Commercial Geography un awamil (factors) ka mutalia karti hai jo dunya mein tijarat (trade), paidawar (production), aur distribution ko mutasir karte hain.

Relationship with other sciences:

  • Economics: Dono ka maqsad profit aur resources ki management hai. Economics batati hai "Kitna" aur Geography batati hai "Kahan".
  • Agriculture: Zameen ki noiyat aur mausam ka faslon par asar Commercial Geography ka hissa hai.
  • History: Purani trade routes aur unki tabdeeli ka mutalia history ke zariye hota hai.

Q2: What is the significance of the Fishing Industry in the economy of Pakistan?

Answer: Mahi-giri (Fishing) Pakistan ki economy mein r रीड ki haddi (backbone) ki hesiyat rakhti hai, khas tor par coastal areas (Karachi, Gawadar) ke liye.

Economic Importance:

  • Employment: Lakhon log direct aur indirect taur par is se wabasta hain.
  • Foreign Exchange: Pakistan prawns, shrimps aur fish export kar ke karoron dollars kamata hai.
  • Food Security: Ye protein ka ek sasta aur behtareen zariya hai.
  • By-products: Machli ke tail (fish oil) aur fertilizer ki manufacturing mein madad milti hai.

Q3: Discuss the types and importance of Natural Resources.

Answer: Natural Resources wo khasayen hain jo qudrat ne insan ko muft faraham ki hain.

Main Types:

  • Renewable Resources: Wo jo kabhi khatam nahi hote (Sunlight, Wind, Water).
  • Non-Renewable Resources: Wo jo istemal ke baad khatam ho jate hain (Coal, Gas, Oil).

Importance: Ye resources kisi bhi mulk ki sanati (industrial) taraqqi ke liye base faraham karte hain. In ke baghair manufacturing mumkin nahi.

Q4: Explain the factors affecting the location of an Industry.

Answer: Kisi bhi jagah factory lagane se pehle darj-e-zail points dekhe jate hain:

  1. Raw Material: Factory kacha maal (raw material) ke qareeb honi chahiye taake transport cost kam ho.
  2. Energy Sources: Bijli aur gas ki musalsal farahmi zaroori hai.
  3. Labor: Sasti aur mahir labour ki dastiyabi.
  4. Market: Market qareeb honi chahiye taake tayyar maal fori bik sakay.
  5. Transport: Roads aur railways ka network hona chahiye.

Q5: Write a note on the Cotton Crop in Pakistan.

Answer: Kapas (Cotton) Pakistan ki "Silver Fiber" kehlati hai aur ye sab se bari cash crop hai.

  • Areas: Punjab (Multan, Bahawalpur) aur Sindh (Hyderabad, Sukkur) iske baray markaz hain.
  • Importance: Pakistan ki textile industry 100% isi par depend karti hai.
  • Exports: Raw cotton aur cotton yarn Pakistan ki export ka sab se bara hissa hain.

Q1: Define Business and explain its main objectives.

Answer: Business ka matlab hai koi bhi aisi legal activity jo profit kamanay ke liye ki jaye.

Objectives of Business:

  • Profit Making: Business ka sab se bara maqsad munafa kamana hota hai taake wo survive kar sakay.
  • Customer Satisfaction: Ache products de kar logon ko mutmain karna.
  • Innovation: Market mein roz naye aur behtar products mutarif karwana.
  • Social Service: Mulk ki economy ko behtar banana aur logon ko jobs dena.

Q2: What is Partnership? Discuss its Advantages and Disadvantages.

Answer: Jab do ya do se zyada log mil kar karobar karte hain aur munafa ya nuqsan baant-te hain, use Partnership kehte hain.

Advantages Disadvantages
More Capital (Zyada Paisa) Unlimited Liability
Shared Risk Chances of Conflict (Larayi ka darr)
Easy to Start Lack of Continuity

Q3: Explain the Importance of Marketing in Modern Business.

Answer: Aaj ke dour mein marketing ke baghair koi bhi business kamyab nahi ho sakta. Is ki ahem wajah ye hai:

  1. Awareness: Logon ko product ke bare mein pata chalta hai.
  2. Sales Increase: Marketing se sales barhti hai aur munafa zyada hota hai.
  3. Competition: Ye market mein doosri companies se muqabla karne mein madad deti hai.
  4. Brand Building: Is se brand ki pehchan banti hai.

Q4: Define "Capital" and its types.

Answer: Wo paisa ya asasa (assets) jo karobar shuru karne ke liye lagaya jaye, Capital kehlata hai.

  • Fixed Capital: Jo lambay arsay ke liye ho (Land, Building, Machinery).
  • Working Capital: Jo roz mara ke kharchon ke liye ho (Cash, Raw material).

Q5: Role of Information Technology (IT) in Business.

Answer: IT ne business karne ka tariqa badal diya hai. Computer aur internet ki wajah se ab "E-commerce" aam ho gaya hai, inventory manage karna asaan hai, aur communication fast ho gayi hai.
